lines.text: Welcome. Today we're talking about Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, by Lewis Carroll, the whole book.
spans: There were doors all round the hall, but they were all locked; and when Alice had been all the way down one side and up the other, trying every door, she walked sadly down the middle, wondering how she was ever to get out again.
For, you see, so many out-of-the-way things had happened lately, that Alice had begun to think that very few things indeed were really impossible.
lines.why: Greeting and naming the work and author; asserts nothing about content.

lines.text: Let's start at the very beginning. How does Alice end up in Wonderland?
spans: The rabbit-hole went straight on like a tunnel for some way, and then dipped suddenly down, so suddenly that Alice had not a moment to think about stopping herself before she found herself falling down a very deep well.
In another moment down went Alice after it, never once considering how in the world she was to get out again.
lines.why: A question presupposing nothing beyond Alice being in Wonderland.

lines.text: A Rabbit takes a watch out of its waistcoat-pocket and looks at it. Alice has never seen a rabbit with a waistcoat-pocket or a watch. She burns with curiosity and runs after it.
spans: I shall be late!” (when she thought it over afterwards, it occurred to her that she ought to have wondered at this, but at the time it all seemed quite natural); but when the Rabbit actually took a watch out of its waistcoat-pocket, and looked at it, and then hurried on, Alice started to her feet, for it flashed across her mind that she had never before seen a rabbit with either a waistcoat-pocket, or a watch to take out of it, and burning with curiosity, she ran across the field after it, and fortunately was just in time to see it pop down a large rabbit-hole under the hedge.
lines.why: Matches S7: watch, waistcoat-pocket, never seen, burning curiosity, ran after it.

lines.text: And then she just jumps in the hole?
spans: In another moment down went Alice after it, never once considering how in the world she was to get out again.
lines.why: S8 says down went Alice after it, consistent with jumping in the hole.

lines.text: Right away. Down she goes, never once considering how in the world she was to get out again. The tunnel dips so suddenly that she finds herself falling down a very deep well.
spans: In another moment down went Alice after it, never once considering how in the world she was to get out again.

The rabbit-hole went straight on like a tunnel for some way, and then dipped suddenly down, so suddenly that Alice had not a moment to think about stopping herself before she found herself falling down a very deep well.
lines.why: Directly matches S8 and S9.

lines.text: What does she find at the bottom?
spans: After a while, finding that nothing more happened, she decided on going into the garden at once; but, alas for poor Alice! when she got to the door, she found she had forgotten the little golden key, and when she went back to the table for it, she found she could not possibly reach it: she could see it quite plainly through the glass, and she tried her best to climb up one of the legs of the table, but it was too slippery; and when she had tired herself out with trying, the poor little thing sat down and cried.

However, on the second time round, she came upon a low curtain she had not noticed before, and behind it was a little door about fifteen inches high: she tried the little golden key in the lock, and to her great delight it fitted!
lines.why: A question presupposing nothing specific beyond something at the bottom.

lines.text: A hall of locked doors. Then a little glass table with a tiny golden key. It fits a door about fifteen inches high, hidden behind a low curtain. Beyond it is the loveliest garden.
spans: There were doors all round the hall, but they were all locked; and when Alice had been all the way down one side and up the other, trying every door, she walked sadly down the middle, wondering how she was ever to get out again.

Suddenly she came upon a little three-legged table, all made of solid glass; there was nothing on it except a tiny golden key, and Alice’s first thought was that it might belong to one of the doors of the hall; but, alas! either the locks were too large, or the key was too small, but at any rate it would not open any of them.

However, on the second time round, she came upon a low curtain she had not noticed before, and behind it was a little door about fifteen inches high: she tried the little golden key in the lock, and to her great delight it fitted!
Alice opened the door and found that it led into a small passage, not much larger than a rat-hole: she knelt down and looked along the passage into the loveliest garden you ever saw.
lines.why: Matches S46-S49: locked doors, glass table, key, small door, garden.

lines.text: But she can't fit through, can she?
spans: How she longed to get out of that dark hall, and wander about among those beds of bright flowers and those cool fountains, but she could not even get her head through the doorway; “and even if my head would go through,” thought poor Alice, “it would be of very little use without my shoulders.
lines.why: A question; its presupposition that she's too big is consistent with S50.

lines.text: No. She can't even get her head through the doorway. Then she finds a bottle with a label that says "DRINK ME," beautifully printed in large letters.
spans: How she longed to get out of that dark hall, and wander about among those beds of bright flowers and those cool fountains, but she could not even get her head through the doorway; “and even if my head would go through,” thought poor Alice, “it would be of very little use without my shoulders.

There seemed to be no use in waiting by the little door, so she went back to the table, half hoping she might find another key on it, or at any rate a book of rules for shutting people up like telescopes: this time she found a little bottle on it, (“which certainly was not here before,” said Alice,) and round the neck of the bottle was a paper label, with the words “DRINK ME,” beautifully printed on it in large letters.
lines.why: S50 head can't get through; S54 bottle with DRINK ME label in large letters.

lines.text: Does she just gulp it down?
spans: It was all very well to say “Drink me,” but the wise little Alice was not going to do that in a hurry.
lines.why: A question presupposing nothing.

lines.text: Not at all. She says, "I'll look first," to see whether it's marked "poison." She remembers the simple rules her friends taught her. It isn't marked, so she tastes it and finds it very nice.
spans: It was all very well to say “Drink me,” but the wise little Alice was not going to do that in a hurry.

“No, I’ll look first,” she said, “and see whether it’s marked ‘poison’ or not”; for she had read several nice little histories about children who had got burnt, and eaten up by wild beasts and other unpleasant things, all because they would not remember the simple rules their friends had taught them: such as, that a red-hot poker will burn you if you hold it too long; and that if you cut your finger very deeply with a knife, it usually bleeds; and she had never forgotten that, if you drink much from a bottle marked “poison,” it is almost certain to disagree with you, sooner or later.

However, this bottle was not marked “poison,” so Alice ventured to taste it, and finding it very nice, (it had, in fact, a sort of mixed flavour of cherry-tart, custard, pine-apple, roast turkey, toffee, and hot buttered toast,) she very soon finished it off.
lines.why: Matches S55-S57: looks first for poison, remembers rules, not marked, tastes nice.

lines.text: What does it taste like?
spans: However, this bottle was not marked “poison,” so Alice ventured to taste it, and finding it very nice, (it had, in fact, a sort of mixed flavour of cherry-tart, custard, pine-apple, roast turkey, toffee, and hot buttered toast,) she very soon finished it off.

“No, I’ll look first,” she said, “and see whether it’s marked ‘poison’ or not”; for she had read several nice little histories about children who had got burnt, and eaten up by wild beasts and other unpleasant things, all because they would not remember the simple rules their friends had taught them: such as, that a red-hot poker will burn you if you hold it too long; and that if you cut your finger very deeply with a knife, it usually bleeds; and she had never forgotten that, if you drink much from a bottle marked “poison,” it is almost certain to disagree with you, sooner or later.
lines.why: A simple question about taste.

lines.text: Cherry-tart, custard, pine-apple, roast turkey, toffee, and hot buttered toast, all mixed together.
spans: However, this bottle was not marked “poison,” so Alice ventured to taste it, and finding it very nice, (it had, in fact, a sort of mixed flavour of cherry-tart, custard, pine-apple, roast turkey, toffee, and hot buttered toast,) she very soon finished it off.
lines.why: Flavours listed exactly in S57.

lines.text: Ha! And then she shrinks?
spans: “What a curious feeling!” said Alice; “I must be shutting up like a telescope.”
And so it was indeed: she was now only ten inches high, and her face brightened up at the thought that she was now the right size for going through the little door into that lovely garden.
lines.why: S61-S62 show she shrinks after drinking.

lines.text: Yes, to ten inches high, the right size for the little door. But she gets nervous. It might end, she says, in her going out altogether, like a candle.
spans: And so it was indeed: she was now only ten inches high, and her face brightened up at the thought that she was now the right size for going through the little door into that lovely garden.

First, however, she waited for a few minutes to see if she was going to shrink any further: she felt a little nervous about this; “for it might end, you know,” said Alice to herself, “in my going out altogether, like a candle.
lines.why: S62 ten inches, right size; S63 nervous, going out like a candle.

lines.text: Poor Alice. Does her size make her doubt who she is?
spans: “I’m afraid I can’t put it more clearly,” Alice replied very politely, “for I can’t understand it myself to begin with; and being so many different sizes in a day is very confusing.”

Luckily for Alice, the little magic bottle had now had its full effect, and she grew no larger: still it was very uncomfortable, and, as there seemed to be no sort of chance of her ever getting out of the room again, no wonder she felt unhappy.
lines.why: A question, with host's sympathy; nothing asserted about the source.

lines.text: Very much. She asks, "Who in the world am I?" and calls it the great puzzle. She wonders if she's been changed in the night.
spans: I wonder if I’ve been changed in the night?
But if I’m not the same, the next question is, Who in the world am I?
lines.why: Matches S105, S108, S109 quotes.

lines.text: How does she test it?
spans: I’ll try and say ‘How doth the little--’” and she crossed her hands on her lap as if she were saying lessons, and began to repeat it, but her voice sounded hoarse and strange, and the words did not come the same as they used to do:--
Alice remained looking thoughtfully at the mushroom for a minute, trying to make out which were the two sides of it; and as it was perfectly round, she found this a very difficult question.
lines.why: A question presupposing nothing beyond a test.

lines.text: She thinks over the children she knows, like Ada and Mabel. Then she tries her lessons. Four times five is twelve, she says, and London is the capital of Paris.
spans: And she began thinking over all the children she knew that were of the same age as herself, to see if she could have been changed for any of them.

“I’m sure I’m not Ada,” she said, “for her hair goes in such long ringlets, and mine doesn’t go in ringlets at all; and I’m sure I can’t be Mabel, for I know all sorts of things, and she, oh! she knows such a very little!
Let me see: four times five is twelve, and four times six is thirteen, and four times seven is--oh dear!
London is the capital of Paris, and Paris is the capital of Rome, and Rome--no, that’s all wrong, I’m certain!
lines.why: Matches S110, S111, S114, S117: Ada, Mabel, four times five twelve, London capital of Paris.

lines.text: So she decides she must be Mabel.
spans: I must have been changed for Mabel!

“I’m sure those are not the right words,” said poor Alice, and her eyes filled with tears again as she went on, “I must be Mabel after all, and I shall have to go and live in that poky little house, and have next to no toys to play with, and oh! ever so many lessons to learn!
lines.why: S118 and S122: Alice concludes she must have been changed for Mabel.

lines.text: She does. Even the poem about the little crocodile comes out wrong, and her voice sounds hoarse and strange.
spans: I’ll try and say ‘How doth the little--’” and she crossed her hands on her lap as if she were saying lessons, and began to repeat it, but her voice sounded hoarse and strange, and the words did not come the same as they used to do:--
“How doth the little crocodile Improve his shining tail, And pour the waters of the Nile On every golden scale!

“I’m sure those are not the right words,” said poor Alice, and her eyes filled with tears again as she went on, “I must be Mabel after all, and I shall have to go and live in that poky little house, and have next to no toys to play with, and oh! ever so many lessons to learn!
lines.why: S119-S122: poem comes out wrong, voice hoarse and strange.

lines.text: Later she goes the other way, right?
spans: It did so indeed, and much sooner than she had expected: before she had drunk half the bottle, she found her head pressing against the ceiling, and had to stoop to save her neck from being broken.
lines.why: A question for clarification; presupposes nothing beyond a transition.

lines.text: She grows so fast that her head presses against the ceiling. Still she keeps growing, and puts one arm out of the window and one foot up the chimney. Then the bottle's effect stops, but there seems no chance of her getting out of the room again.
spans: It did so indeed, and much sooner than she had expected: before she had drunk half the bottle, she found her head pressing against the ceiling, and had to stoop to save her neck from being broken.
Still she went on growing, and, as a last resource, she put one arm out of the window, and one foot up the chimney, and said to herself “Now I can do no more, whatever happens.

Luckily for Alice, the little magic bottle had now had its full effect, and she grew no larger: still it was very uncomfortable, and, as there seemed to be no sort of chance of her ever getting out of the room again, no wonder she felt unhappy.
lines.why: Head against ceiling, arm out window, foot up chimney supported; 'can't get out' is only implied by S308 but 'grows so fast' fine; she stops growing is omitted but ok. Main points hold, though 'In the end' glosses stopping.
lines.was: She grows so fast that her head presses against the ceiling. In the end she puts one arm out of the window and one foot up the chimney. She still can't get out of the room.

lines.text: And then she meets the Caterpillar.
spans: The Caterpillar and Alice looked at each other for some time in silence: at last the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth, and addressed her in a languid, sleepy voice.
lines.why: S399 shows Alice and the Caterpillar meeting and looking at each other.

lines.text: He asks, "Who are you?" She says she hardly knows. She knew who she was that morning, but she's been changed several times since.
spans: Alice replied, rather shyly, “I--I hardly know, sir, just at present--at least I know who I was when I got up this morning, but I think I must have been changed several times since then.”
lines.why: S400 and S402 match the question and Alice's reply.

lines.text: Does he understand?
spans: “I’m afraid I can’t put it more clearly,” Alice replied very politely, “for I can’t understand it myself to begin with; and being so many different sizes in a day is very confusing.”
lines.why: A question presupposing nothing substantive about the source.

lines.text: No. She says, "I'm not myself, you see." He answers, "I don't see." She says being so many different sizes in a day is very confusing. He says it isn't.
spans: “I can’t explain myself, I’m afraid, sir,” said Alice, “because I’m not myself, you see.”
“I’m afraid I can’t put it more clearly,” Alice replied very politely, “for I can’t understand it myself to begin with; and being so many different sizes in a day is very confusing.”
lines.why: S405-S408 match the exchange: not myself, I don't see, confusing, it isn't.

lines.text: Does he give her any help?
spans: The other side of what?” thought Alice to herself.
It did so indeed, and much sooner than she had expected: before she had drunk half the bottle, she found her head pressing against the ceiling, and had to stoop to save her neck from being broken.
lines.why: A question that presupposes nothing beyond a transition.

lines.text: Before he crawls away, he says one side of the mushroom will make her grow taller and the other side shorter. She then breaks off a bit of the edge with each hand.
spans: Then it got down off the mushroom, and crawled away in the grass, merely remarking as it went, “One side will make you grow taller, and the other side will make you grow shorter.”
“Of the mushroom,” said the Caterpillar, just as if she had asked it aloud; and in another moment it was out of sight.
However, at last she stretched her arms round it as far as they would go, and broke off a bit of the edge with each hand.
lines.why: Mushroom sides and breaking pieces supported; 'from each edge' is slightly off, she broke a bit of the edge with each hand.
lines.was: Before he crawls away, he says one side of the mushroom will make her taller and the other shorter. She breaks off a bit from each edge with each hand.

lines.text: Does the mushroom work?
spans: After a while she remembered that she still held the pieces of mushroom in her hands, and she set to work very carefully, nibbling first at one and then at the other, and growing sometimes taller and sometimes shorter, until she had succeeded in bringing herself down to her usual height.
So she set the little creature down, and felt quite relieved to see it trot away quietly into the wood.
lines.why: A question that presupposes nothing.

lines.text: It does. She nibbles first one piece, then the other, until she's back to her usual height. Then she says, "there's half my plan done now."
spans: After a while she remembered that she still held the pieces of mushroom in her hands, and she set to work very carefully, nibbling first at one and then at the other, and growing sometimes taller and sometimes shorter, until she had succeeded in bringing herself down to her usual height.
“Come, there’s half my plan done now!
lines.why: S507 and S509 match nibbling, usual height, and half the plan done.

lines.text: And the other half?
spans: However, I’ve got back to my right size: the next thing is, to get into that beautiful garden--how is that to be done, I wonder?”
lines.why: A question that presupposes nothing.

lines.text: To get into that beautiful garden. Instead she comes upon a little house about four feet high.
spans: However, I’ve got back to my right size: the next thing is, to get into that beautiful garden--how is that to be done, I wonder?”
As she said this, she came suddenly upon an open place, with a little house in it about four feet high.
lines.why: S512 and S513: the garden is next; she comes upon a house four feet high.

lines.text: I hear there's a baby that turns into something.
spans: After a while she remembered that she still held the pieces of mushroom in her hands, and she set to work very carefully, nibbling first at one and then at the other, and growing sometimes taller and sometimes shorter, until she had succeeded in bringing herself down to her usual height.
“If it had grown up,” she said to herself, “it would have made a dreadfully ugly child: but it makes rather a handsome pig, I think.”
lines.why: Host's tease or question about a baby; asserts nothing about the source content.

lines.text: A pig. It grunts violently, and there's no mistake about it. Alice sets it down and feels relieved to see it trot quietly into the wood.
spans: Alice was just beginning to think to herself, “Now, what am I to do with this creature when I get it home?” when it grunted again, so violently, that she looked down into its face in some alarm.
This time there could be no mistake about it: it was neither more nor less than a pig, and she felt that it would be quite absurd for her to carry it further.
So she set the little creature down, and felt quite relieved to see it trot away quietly into the wood.
lines.why: S604-S606 match the grunting, pig, setting it down, and trotting into the wood.

lines.text: Then she sees the Cheshire Cat.
spans: And she began thinking over other children she knew, who might do very well as pigs, and was just saying to herself, “if one only knew the right way to change them--” when she was a little startled by seeing the Cheshire Cat sitting on a bough of a tree a few yards off.
lines.why: S608: she is startled by seeing the Cheshire Cat on a bough.

lines.text: Sitting on a bough of a tree. She asks what sort of people live nearby. It waves a paw each way. A Hatter lives one way, a March Hare the other.
spans: And she began thinking over other children she knew, who might do very well as pigs, and was just saying to herself, “if one only knew the right way to change them--” when she was a little startled by seeing the Cheshire Cat sitting on a bough of a tree a few yards off.
“What sort of people live about here?”
“In that direction,” the Cat said, waving its right paw round, “lives a Hatter: and in that direction,” waving the other paw, “lives a March Hare.
lines.why: Cat on bough, Alice asks, paws point to Hatter and March Hare.

lines.text: And they're friendly?
spans: Visit either you like: they’re both mad.”
“What sort of people live about here?”
lines.why: A question asking if they're friendly; presupposes nothing about the source.

lines.text: The Cat says they're both mad. Alice doesn't want mad people. The Cat says, "we're all mad here." Even Alice, because she wouldn't have come here otherwise.
spans: Visit either you like: they’re both mad.”
“But I don’t want to go among mad people,” Alice remarked.
“Oh, you can’t help that,” said the Cat: “we’re all mad here.
“You must be,” said the Cat, “or you wouldn’t have come here.”
lines.why: Cat says both mad, Alice objects, Cat says all mad, Alice must be or wouldn't have come.

lines.text: What's the Hatter's story about time?
lines.why: A question about the Hatter's story; asserts nothing.

lines.text: At the Queen of Hearts' great concert, he had to sing "Twinkle, twinkle, little bat." He'd hardly finished the first verse when the Queen bawled, "He's murdering the time! Off with his head!"
spans: “We quarrelled last March--just before he went mad, you know--” (pointing with his tea spoon at the March Hare,) “--it was at the great concert given by the Queen of Hearts, and I had to sing
“Well, I’d hardly finished the first verse,” said the Hatter, “when the Queen jumped up and bawled out, ‘He’s murdering the time!
lines.why: Concert, singing Twinkle, hardly finished first verse, Queen bawled 'murdering the time'.

lines.text: Yikes. What happened after that?
spans: Alice was just beginning to think to herself, “Now, what am I to do with this creature when I get it home?” when it grunted again, so violently, that she looked down into its face in some alarm.
lines.why: Reaction and a question; asserts nothing about the source.

lines.text: Ever since, he says, Time won't do a thing he asks. It's always six o'clock now.
spans: “And ever since that,” the Hatter went on in a mournful tone, “he won’t do a thing I ask!
lines.why: Hatter says ever since, he won't do a thing; always six o'clock.

lines.text: Let's jump to the Queen's court. How does Alice handle her?
spans: “Nonsense!” said Alice, very loudly and decidedly, and the Queen was silent.
“Idiot!” said the Queen, tossing her head impatiently; and, turning to Alice, she went on, “What’s your name, child?”
lines.why: Transition and question; no claim about the source content.

lines.text: Politely at first. "My name is Alice, so please your Majesty." But she tells herself, "they're only a pack of cards, after all. I needn't be afraid of them!"
spans: “My name is Alice, so please your Majesty,” said Alice very politely; but she added, to herself, “Why, they’re only a pack of cards, after all.
I needn’t be afraid of them!”
lines.why: Alice says name politely, then tells herself they're only a pack of cards.

lines.text: And then she gets bolder.
spans: “How should I know?” said Alice, surprised at her own courage.
lines.why: Alice 'surprised at her own courage' supports getting bolder.

lines.text: The Queen asks about the three gardeners. Alice says, "It's no business of mine," surprised at her own courage. The Queen screams, "Off with her head!"
spans: “And who are these?” said the Queen, pointing to the three gardeners who were lying round the rose-tree; for, you see, as they were lying on their faces, and the pattern on their backs was the same as the rest of the pack, she could not tell whether they were gardeners, or soldiers, or courtiers, or three of her own children.
“How should I know?” said Alice, surprised at her own courage.
The Queen turned crimson with fury, and, after glaring at her for a moment like a wild beast, screamed “Off with her head!
lines.why: Queen asks about gardeners, Alice replies, surprised at courage; Queen screams 'Off with her head!'

lines.text: Yikes. What does Alice do?
spans: “Wake up, Alice dear!” said her sister; “Why, what a long sleep you’ve had!”

“Oh, I’ve had such a curious dream!” said Alice, and she told her sister, as well as she could remember them, all these strange Adventures of hers that you have just been reading about; and when she had finished, her sister kissed her, and said, “It was a curious dream, dear, certainly: but now run in to your tea; it’s getting late.”
lines.why: Reaction and question; asserts nothing about the source.

lines.text: She says "Nonsense!" very loudly and decidedly, and the Queen is silent. The King timidly says, "Consider, my dear: she is only a child!"
spans: “Nonsense!” said Alice, very loudly and decidedly, and the Queen was silent.
The King laid his hand upon her arm, and timidly said “Consider, my dear: she is only a child!”
lines.why: Alice says 'Nonsense!', Queen silent, King timidly says 'Consider, my dear'.

lines.text: What about the poor gardeners?
spans: “Off with their heads!” and the procession moved on, three of the soldiers remaining behind to execute the unfortunate gardeners, who ran to Alice for protection.
lines.why: A question about the gardeners; presupposes nothing beyond the source.

lines.text: The Queen sees the roses and says, "Off with their heads!" The gardeners run to Alice. She puts them into a large flower-pot. The soldiers search, then march off.
spans: “I see!” said the Queen, who had meanwhile been examining the roses.
“Off with their heads!” and the procession moved on, three of the soldiers remaining behind to execute the unfortunate gardeners, who ran to Alice for protection.
“You shan’t be beheaded!” said Alice, and she put them into a large flower-pot that stood near.
The three soldiers wandered about for a minute or two, looking for them, and then quietly marched off after the others.
lines.why: Queen sees roses, orders beheading, gardeners run to Alice, flower-pot, soldiers search and leave.

lines.text: And the Queen believes the heads are gone.
spans: “Are their heads off?” shouted the Queen.
“Their heads are gone, if it please your Majesty!” the soldiers shouted in reply.
lines.why: Queen asks if heads are off and is told they're gone, replying 'That's right!'.

lines.text: Yes. The soldiers shout, "Their heads are gone," and the Queen shouts, "That's right!"
spans: “Their heads are gone, if it please your Majesty!” the soldiers shouted in reply.
lines.why: Soldiers shout heads are gone; Queen shouts 'That's right!'.

lines.text: How does it all end?
spans: At this the whole pack rose up into the air, and came flying down upon her: she gave a little scream, half of fright and half of anger, and tried to beat them off, and found herself lying on the bank, with her head in the lap of her sister, who was gently brushing away some dead leaves that had fluttered down from the trees upon her face.
“Off with their heads!” and the procession moved on, three of the soldiers remaining behind to execute the unfortunate gardeners, who ran to Alice for protection.
lines.why: A question asking how it ends; asserts nothing.

lines.text: Alice, now full size, says, "You're nothing but a pack of cards!" The whole pack rises into the air and flies down upon her.
spans: “Who cares for you?” said Alice, (she had grown to her full size by this time.)
“You’re nothing but a pack of cards!”

At this the whole pack rose up into the air, and came flying down upon her: she gave a little scream, half of fright and half of anger, and tried to beat them off, and found herself lying on the bank, with her head in the lap of her sister, who was gently brushing away some dead leaves that had fluttered down from the trees upon her face.
lines.why: Matches S1421-S1423: full size, the quote, pack rises and flies down upon her.

lines.text: And then she wakes up?
spans: At this the whole pack rose up into the air, and came flying down upon her: she gave a little scream, half of fright and half of anger, and tried to beat them off, and found herself lying on the bank, with her head in the lap of her sister, who was gently brushing away some dead leaves that had fluttered down from the trees upon her face.
lines.why: S1423 shows she finds herself on the bank, implying waking; question presupposes little.

lines.text: She finds herself on the bank, her head in her sister's lap. Her sister is brushing dead leaves from her face. Alice says, "I've had such a curious dream!"
spans: At this the whole pack rose up into the air, and came flying down upon her: she gave a little scream, half of fright and half of anger, and tried to beat them off, and found herself lying on the bank, with her head in the lap of her sister, who was gently brushing away some dead leaves that had fluttered down from the trees upon her face.

“Oh, I’ve had such a curious dream!” said Alice, and she told her sister, as well as she could remember them, all these strange Adventures of hers that you have just been reading about; and when she had finished, her sister kissed her, and said, “It was a curious dream, dear, certainly: but now run in to your tea; it’s getting late.”
lines.why: S1423 and S1425 support the bank, sister's lap, leaves, and the dream quote.

lines.text: What does the sister think of it?
spans: Lastly, she pictured to herself how this same little sister of hers would, in the after-time, be herself a grown woman; and how she would keep, through all her riper years, the simple and loving heart of her childhood: and how she would gather about her other little children, and make their eyes bright and eager with many a strange tale, perhaps even with the dream of Wonderland of long ago: and how she would feel with all their simple sorrows, and find a pleasure in all their simple joys, remembering her own child-life, and the happy summer days.

“Oh, I’ve had such a curious dream!” said Alice, and she told her sister, as well as she could remember them, all these strange Adventures of hers that you have just been reading about; and when she had finished, her sister kissed her, and said, “It was a curious dream, dear, certainly: but now run in to your tea; it’s getting late.”
lines.why: A question presupposing nothing beyond the sister's reaction; asserts no source content.

lines.text: She sits with closed eyes and half believes herself in Wonderland. Then she pictures her little sister grown, keeping the simple and loving heart of her childhood.
spans: So she sat on, with closed eyes, and half believed herself in Wonderland, though she knew she had but to open them again, and all would change to dull reality--the grass would be only rustling in the wind, and the pool rippling to the waving of the reeds--the rattling teacups would change to tinkling sheep-bells, and the Queen’s shrill cries to the voice of the shepherd boy--and the sneeze of the baby, the shriek of the Gryphon, and all the other queer noises, would change (she knew) to the confused clamour of the busy farm-yard--while the lowing of the cattle in the distance would take the place of the Mock Turtle’s heavy sobs.

Lastly, she pictured to herself how this same little sister of hers would, in the after-time, be herself a grown woman; and how she would keep, through all her riper years, the simple and loving heart of her childhood: and how she would gather about her other little children, and make their eyes bright and eager with many a strange tale, perhaps even with the dream of Wonderland of long ago: and how she would feel with all their simple sorrows, and find a pleasure in all their simple joys, remembering her own child-life, and the happy summer days.
lines.why: Closed eyes and half-believing are supported, but the sister pictures her own self grown, not Alice.
lines.was: She sits with closed eyes and half believes herself in Wonderland. She pictures Alice grown, keeping the simple and loving heart of her childhood.

lines.text: What would grown-up Alice do?
spans: “Who cares for you?” said Alice, (she had grown to her full size by this time.)
“Wake up, Alice dear!” said her sister; “Why, what a long sleep you’ve had!”
lines.why: A question presupposing nothing unsupported; it only asks what grown-up Alice would do.

lines.text: She'd gather other little children about her and make their eyes bright with strange tales, perhaps even the dream of Wonderland. She'd feel their simple sorrows and joys, remembering her own child-life and the happy summer days.

lines.was: Gather other little children and tell them strange tales, perhaps even the dream of Wonderland. She would share their sorrows and joys, remembering the happy summer days.
